title: Toward an Atlas of Cultural Commonsense for Machine Reasoning
base_benchmarks: College Students Knowledge and Belief (Clark and Barrows 1981) questionnaire
findings: The study's key finding is that cultural commonsense about rituals, which is often intertwined with religion, varies significantly across national groups. For example, survey responses from India regarding weddings placed a greater emphasis on religious and ritualistic aspects, while responses from the US focused more on the social celebration (party). The paper also noted demographic differences, with US participants showing more religious diversity and a greater tendency to change their religious affiliation over their lifetime compared to Indian participants. For funerals, US participants were more likely to mention a pastor or priest as an important figure, whereas Indian participants focused more on family.

measurement_description: The study collected data on cultural commonsense knowledge surrounding six universal life rituals (birth, coming-of-age, marriage, funerals, new year, birthdays). This included measuring the religious diversity of participants and understanding the role and expression of religious practices within these rituals across different cultural groups (specifically, from the US and India).
